messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 47
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Park Ranger
- Trauma Type: Civilian in war zone
- Pcl5: 74

He is 47, an African man who has spent most of his adult life outdoors, and even now he works as a park ranger, preferring long patrols and quiet terrain to offices or crowds. When he begins telling his story, he does so carefully, as if each detail has to be handled without disturbing something dangerous underneath.

He grows up in a rural area where the land is familiar, where people know the trails, the seasons, the sounds of animals at night. Before the war reaches him directly, he remembers himself as steady and capable, someone others rely on. He helps his family, works hard, and imagines a future that is ordinary in the best way. Then the fighting moves closer. At first it is rumor and distance—stories of villages attacked, men taken, bodies found by roadsides. He learns to listen for changes in the air. He notices how quickly daily life narrows around fear.

The event he returns to most often happens when he is in his early adulthood. Armed men enter his community without warning. There is shouting, then gunfire, then the kind of chaos that makes it impossible to think in a straight line. He remembers running, dropping to the ground, the smell of dust and smoke mixing together. He sees people he knows falling. He hears a woman screaming for her child. At one point he hides among brush and lies so still that insects crawl over his arms and face. He believes that if he breathes too loudly, he will be found and killed. From where he is hiding, he sees bodies left in open ground. He cannot go to them. He cannot help anyone. That helplessness remains with him as sharply as the fear.

Afterward, he survives by moving from place to place, staying alert, sleeping lightly, trusting almost no one. Even when the immediate danger passes, his body does not seem to understand that it has passed. He startles violently at sudden noise. If a car backfires, his chest seizes before he can remind himself where he is. For years, he avoids talking about what he saw. When relatives or friends try to bring up that period, he leaves the room or finds work to do. He tells himself that silence is strength. Instead, the memories come on their own.

He describes nights as the worst. Sleep is shallow and broken. Some nights he jerks awake already sweating, certain he has heard boots or voices outside. In dreams, he is back on the ground in the brush, unable to move, listening for footsteps. Other times he sees again the faces of those he could not save. When he wakes, he often gets up immediately to check doors and windows, then sits for long stretches in the dark, unable to settle. By morning he is exhausted and irritable, and small frustrations feel bigger than they should.

His work as a park ranger suits him in some ways. He is competent, observant, and highly attuned to the environment. He can read tracks, notice what is out of place, and remain calm in difficult terrain. Colleagues respect how seriously he takes safety. But the same vigilance that helps him on patrol also consumes him. He scans constantly. He prefers routes that give him a clear line of sight. Dense brush, where someone could hide, makes his shoulders tighten. If he encounters armed personnel, even in legitimate security roles, his stomach drops and his mind begins preparing for attack before he can stop it. He knows the difference between then and now, but his body reacts as though there is none.

Outside work, his life has grown smaller over time. He is single and says relationships become difficult because he keeps too much inside. He does not like sitting with his back to a door in cafés or meetings. He avoids celebrations, markets, and crowded transport. Loud voices make him tense, even when people are only joking. There are periods when he feels emotionally cut off, watching others laugh or relax as if from a great distance. He sometimes wonders whether the part of him that once felt close to people was left behind there, in the violence he survived.

He carries guilt that does not respond to reason. He knows he was a civilian, unarmed, outnumbered, and trying to stay alive. Still, he thinks often of those who died and asks himself why he is here when others are not. On some days, the guilt comes as a heavy quiet. On others, it turns into anger—at the men who attacked, at the world that continued, at himself for surviving by hiding.

In the present, he remains dependable and disciplined, a man who keeps going to work, keeps his routines, and does what is required of him. Yet his days are organized around anticipation of danger and his nights around escape from memory. He speaks with control, but the cost of that control is visible: the fixed posture, the rapid glance toward any unexpected sound, the long pauses when the past presses close. Even in the safety of the consulting room, he seems to live partly in the war zone still, measuring distance to exits, listening for threat, and carrying a history his nervous system has never stopped expecting to repeat.
